children: As deployment crosses 7 crore, utilities are working to convert meter data into measurable gains across power procurement and network operations

India’s smart-meter programme has moved from the pilot phase as the power sector shifts its focus from installing millions of smart meters to using the data generated by them to improve distribution operations, forecasting, asset management and consumer services.

More than 7 crore smart meters have been installed, according to Shashank Misra, Joint Secretary (Distribution), Ministry of Power. However, the scale of deployment has also created a new challenge: how to convert the growing volume of meter data into measurable value for consumers and distribution companies (DISCOMs).

The issue predominantly resonated at the 11th edition of Metering India 2026, where policymakers and distribution utilities discussed the next phase of India’s smart-meter programme. The discussions pointed to a shift in priorities, from building smart-meter infrastructure to converting the information generated by that infrastructure into operational and consumer benefits.

Power Grid Corporation of India’s (PGCIL) 2.5 million smart-meter phase, tendered as part of the broader national smart-metering programme, illustrates the scale of the deployment effort. The experience of utilities, however, suggests that the value of the programme will ultimately depend on what happens after the meters are installed.
7 Crore Meters, New Challenge

The government now sees the volume of data generated by smart meters as both an opportunity and a challenge. “Smart metering is currently navigating a critical phase. With nearly 7 crore smart meters already deployed, we are generating an unprecedented volume of data,” said Shashank Misra, Joint Secretary (Distribution), Ministry of Power. The scale of deployment has not translated into equivalent consumer engagement.

Misra said fewer than 20 per cent of consumers with smart meters are downloading or using the associated applications. He said the gap needs to be addressed if consumers are to see the benefits of smart metering. “If the consumers are not using the app, if the consumers are not finding the app worthwhile, then, you know, it could not be a holistic effort,” he added.
Data Must Deliver Value

For distribution companies, the question is increasingly whether investment in smart metering can translate into measurable gains. “The objective is to make use of the data, improving the efficiency and productivity of the DISCOM, rendering better services to the consumers. Consumers should see the value,” said Abhishek Ranjan, CEO, BRPL.

“If it can't be quantified, then the interest will not be there. It has to be seen that the measurable, tangible, quantified benefits are there on the table, so that the real payback can be computed for the investment made in this market,” said Ranjan. The point is particularly relevant for utilities that have already achieved high collection efficiency and relatively low distribution losses. He pointed to battery storage, flexible electric vehicle charging, rooftop solar, smart inverters and controllable appliances as assets that could help utilities unlock greater flexibility.
Utilities Put Data To Work

The potential use of smart-meter data extends beyond billing and conventional loss reduction. “The flexibility that is required, how I am using the data to create insights for better power procurement, for better forecasting, for better network management, network planning, asset management,” said Dwijadas Basak, CEO, Tata Power Delhi Distribution.

Basak also identified predictive maintenance as an important application. He said the challenge is to use data to move from reactive maintenance towards proactive and predictive maintenance. The shift changes the role of the smart meter. Instead of functioning only as a device that records electricity consumption, it becomes a source of continuous information that can feed operational decisions across the distribution network.
Turning Data Into Grid Intelligence

The frequency of the data is also changing what utilities can see. “Smart meters are the backbone of DISCOM operations,” said Santosh Kumar, COO, BYPL. Kumar said smart meters communicate data every 15 minutes, allowing utilities to apply analytics to the information generated.

The data provides utilities with visibility into loading patterns, power factor, power quality, voltage imbalance, current imbalance and losses. The utility also maps consumers and distribution transformers through geographic information system (GIS) platforms and uses its outage-management system to identify voltage profiles and transformers carrying loads above their designated levels. These applications illustrate the larger transition underway. Smart meters are becoming an input into utility decision-making systems rather than merely devices that record consumption.
From Data To Action

The government’s concern about consumer adoption also extends to the field level. Misra questioned what DISCOM engineers are actually getting from smart-meter data and whether the information provides direct insights that can improve their work. He said the sector needs to strengthen the data component of smart metering. “We need to strongly now develop and work upon the data part of smart meter,” said Misra.

He also pointed out that the large number of junior engineers working in the field should become “foot soldiers” for the benefits of smart metering once they can see the value of the data. This points to a gap between data generation and data utilisation. A smart-meter network can generate granular information every few minutes, but the investment creates greater value only when that information changes a decision, whether it is a consumer adjusting consumption, a DISCOM forecasting demand, a utility identifying an overloaded transformer, or an engineer responding to a network problem.

That makes the next phase of India’s smart-meter programme different from the first. The first challenge was to create digital metering infrastructure at scale. With more than 7 crore meters already installed, the emerging challenge is to make that infrastructure economically and operationally productive.

For the government, that means improving consumer engagement and making applications useful enough for consumers to adopt them. For DISCOMs, it means converting meter data into measurable improvements in procurement, forecasting, network planning, asset management and maintenance. The scale of India’s smart-meter programme has therefore created a new test for the power sector: whether millions of connected meters can become a source of actionable intelligence rather than simply a larger source of electricity data.
Kapil Saini
